title: Shortest runs in 3-D VASS
formal: Is there no single-exponential bound on shortest runs in binary-encoded three-dimensional vector addition systems with states? Precisely, is it true that for every integer \(k\ge 1\), every real \(C>0\) and every \(N_{0}\ge 1\), there is a reachable instance I of encoding length \(N\ge N_{0}\) whose shortest source-to-target run has more than \(2^{C N^{k}}\) transitions?
why: Isolates how much witness complexity three unbounded counters can force. Resolving the single-exponential threshold would clarify the gap between low-dimensional reachability and the much more expensive behavior possible when the number of counters grows.
status_note: Original question and the 2025 explicit binary formulation checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 preprint improves the upper bound but does not resolve whether single-exponential shortest runs always suffice. No resolution of that threshold was located; proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Czerwiński asks for a three-counter shortest-run lower bound beyond the exponential scale; the upper-bound discussion is historical.
The ICALP paper obtains a triple-exponential shortest-run upper bound and 2-EXPSPACE membership. Section 7 retains the question whether single-exponential runs suffice for binary 3-VASS.

Chen and coauthors state a doubly-exponential shortest-run upper bound and EXPSPACE membership in a new preprint. This review checked the model and theorem statements, not the full proof; the result does not supply the requested super-single-exponential lower bound.

sentences: A three-dimensional VASS is a finite-state system with three nonnegative integer counters.
The source asks whether some reachable instances require shortest runs longer than every single-exponential bound in their binary input length.
Encoding a large initial counter in binary already permits exponentially many necessary steps, so a stronger growth rate is required.
A July 2026 preprint states a doubly-exponential upper bound, improving the triple-exponential bound from 2025.
The remaining threshold question measures how much reachability-witness complexity three counters can force.

definitions: A three-dimensional vector addition system with states (3-VASS) is a finite set Q of control states and a finite transition set \(T\subseteq Q\times \mathbb{Z} ^{3}\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,u)\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(u\in \mathbb{N} ^{3}\), where \(\mathbb{N}\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q' )\) sends \((q,u)\) to \((q' ,u+a)\) only when every coordinate of \(u+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests or counter bounds. A reachability instance I consists of Q,T and two configurations s,t. It is reachable if some finite sequence of enabled transitions sends s to t. Its shortest-run length \(\ell\)\((I)\) is the minimum number of transitions in such a sequence; the empty run is allowed, and \(\ell\)\((I)=0\) when \(s=t\). Unreachable instances are excluded from the quantified claim. N is the bit length of an explicit description: states are numbered, the transition list and the source and target are given explicitly, and all integer coordinates are written in signed binary (nonnegative binary for configurations), with delimiters and state indices included. Usual explicit binary-list encodings differ by polynomial factors, which do not affect existence of a \(2^{N^{O}(1)}\) bound. The dimension is always exactly three, while the number of states, transitions and counter magnitudes may grow. No finite-reachability-set promise or effective construction of the hard instances is required. The single-exponential convention and binary encoding follow the explicit later formulation in Section 7 of the 2025 source.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed unboundedness beyond every \(2^{C N^{k}}\), or refute it by proving that there are fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge 1\) for which every reachable binary 3-VASS instance I has \(\ell\)\((I)\le 2^{C |I|^{k}}\), after adjusting C to include the finitely many small sizes. A long run alone is insufficient: the lower bound concerns the shortest run between the chosen configurations. Neither a lower bound with a growing number of counters nor the mere existence of many reachable configurations establishes this target.

context_blocks.title: Three counters, infinitely many configurations
context_blocks.text: The control graph is finite, but each counter may become arbitrarily large. A transition can consume tokens from one counter and produce tokens in another, provided it never makes a counter negative. Reachability asks whether a target configuration can be obtained from a given start through legal transitions.

context_blocks.title: Why the binary encoding matters
context_blocks.text: Consider one state and the single transition \((- 1,+1,0)\), from counters \((2^{r},0,0)\) to \((0,2^{r},0)\). Every successful run has exactly \(2^{r}\) steps, although the instance uses only \(O(r)\) bits. This gives exponential length in the input description. The question asks whether shortest runs can exceed every bound \(2^{N^{k}}\), with fixed k, rather than merely whether exponential runs occur.

context_blocks.title: Shortest paths control witness size
context_blocks.text: A reachable target may have many very long runs leading to it. Only the minimum length is relevant here. A single-exponential shortest-run upper bound would allow the binary reachability problem to be decided in polynomial space, as the 2025 source explains. A lower bound on the number or largest size of reachable configurations is a different assertion.

context_blocks.title: The known upper bound has changed
context_blocks.text: The 2019 question mentioned a tower-type upper bound. The ICALP 2025 work gives a triple-exponential bound on shortest runs, and the July 2026 preprint states an improvement to a doubly-exponential bound. These upper bounds do not establish that any shortest run actually needs more than single-exponential length.
